t: That the paragraph under the head, “United States Maritime Commission” in title I of the Third Deficiency Appropriation Act, 1946 (Public Law 521, Seventy-ninth Congress, approved July 23, 1946), as amended by section 2 of Public Law 6, Eightieth Congress, approved February 26, 1947, and section 1 of said Public Law 6, Eightieth Congress, and the first two sentences of section 11 (a) and section 14 of the Merchant Ship Sales Act of 1946 (Public Law 321, Seventy-ninth Congress, approved March 8, 1946), are amended by striking out the dates “July 1, 1947” and “December 31, 1947”, wherever either appear therein, and inserting in lieu thereof the date “March 1, 1948”.

fable.w: This section only extends statutory dates in earlier Maritime Commission and Merchant Ship Sales Act provisions by substituting a new date. The tempting reading is that references to the Maritime Commission or ship sales imply dealings with outside parties, but the text sets up no consultation, hearing, rulemaking, advisory body, or right to sue. No party outside the federal government is brought into any federal decision.
fable.s: wherever either appear therein, and inserting in lieu thereof the date

qwen_block.w: This section is a technical amendment to an appropriations act, extending a deadline from December 31, 1947, to March 1, 1948. It does not establish any process for consultation, public comment, advisory boards, or coordination with outside parties. It is purely an administrative change to statutory dates.
qwen_block.s: That the paragraph under the head, “United States Maritime Commission” in title I of the Third Deficiency Appropriation Act, 1946... are amended by striking out the dates “July 1, 1947” and “December 31, 1947”, wherever either appear therein, and inserting in lieu thereof the date “March 1, 1948”.

opus.w: This section only extends deadlines in earlier appropriations and ship-sales laws by replacing old dates with March 1, 1948. It does not require or allow the federal government to consult or coordinate with anyone outside the government before a decision. It also creates no hearing, comment period, advisory committee, rulemaking authority, or right to sue. The link to ship sales involving private buyers is only background and puts no outside party into any federal decision.
opus.s: are amended by striking out the dates “July 1, 1947” and “December 31, 1947”, wherever either appear therein, and inserting in lieu thereof the date “March 1, 1948”.
opus.b:
1. **The tempting reading and why it fails:** The section changes deadlines in the Merchant Ship Sales Act, and that Act covers selling ships to private buyers. You could guess that buyers or the public have some role in it. But the section itself only swaps dates. It creates no hearing, comment period, advisory body, consultation with outsiders, rulemaking authority, or right to sue.

qwen_chat.w: This section is a technical amendment to existing statutes, specifically changing expiration or effective dates from 1947 to 1948. It does not establish any process for consultation, coordination, or participation with entities outside the federal government. The only actors mentioned are the United States Maritime Commission (a federal agency) and Congress (which enacted the amendment), both of which are inside the federal government.
qwen_chat.s: That the paragraph under the head, “United States Maritime Commission” in title I of the Third Deficiency Appropriation Act, 1946... are amended by striking out the dates “July 1, 1947” and “December 31, 1947”, wherever either appear therein, and inserting in lieu thereof the date “March 1, 1948”.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that changing dates in a statute involving the Maritime Commission implies some procedural change or consultation, but the text is purely an amendment of effective dates for existing statutory provisions. There is no mention of consulting with outside parties, holding hearings, or involving non-federal entities in a decision-making process. The actors involved are Congress (amending the law) and the federal agency (Maritime Commission), both inside the government.
